reasoning: The Titanic data has a binary target (Survived) and mixed numeric/categorical features. High‑cardinality free‑text columns (Name, Ticket, Cabin) risk over‑fitting, so we extract concise signals and then drop the raw text. • Name: capture the passenger title (e.g. Mr, Mrs, Miss) with a regex; titles are known strong predictors of survival. • Cabin: extract the deck letter (first character) which encodes location on the ship and is far less sparse than the full cabin code (77 % missing). • Ticket: extract any alphabetic prefix (e.g. “PC”, “A/5”) that groups tickets bought together. We also create a group‑size feature for Ticket to capture families or groups sharing a ticket. • Fare is highly right‑skewed (skew = 4.79) so we log‑transform it. • Age has ~20 % missing; we keep the column (imputation will be handled downstream) and add a missing‑indicator (default true). • Embarked, Sex and Pclass are low‑cardinality categoricals; we frequency‑encode them to give tree models a numeric representation without one‑hot explosion. • Ticket and Cabin (raw) are dropped after extracting the deck/prefix and group‑size, as they provide little additional signal beyond the engineered features. PassengerId is a pure identifier and is also dropped. No datetime columns exist. The target is binary, so we do not log‑transform it. This plan directly addresses the listed risks: class imbalance is handled by model choice, missing Age is flagged, and high‑cardinality text is reduced to compact categorical signals.
